title: Allocation & saturation probe: throughput vs quality for INT8 / AWQ / FP8
content:
Purpose:
Run focused experiments to tease apart two related failure modes we keep hitting in production: (1) throughput plateauing despite unused compute headroom and (2) intermittent quality regressions when switching kernels/quant formats during sustained bursts. Hypothesis is that memory allocator saturation + kernel packing decisions interact badly with small variable-length batches (prefix heavy), causing micro-fragmentation and kernel dispatch hot-path contention.

Context / motivation:
- Recent customer reports (SRV-987) show >20% tail latency spikes under mixed short/long prompt mixes on AWQ-int8 variants; FP8 didn’t spike but showed slightly worse quality in long-context regeneration tests.
- We suspect not only numerical quant tradeoffs but also resource allocation (per-stream scratch buffers, reuse patterns) cause throughput cliff.
- Goal: produce a reproducible microbenchmark + profiler traces that pinpoint if saturation is allocator/memory-bandwidth/dispatcher limited, and quantify the quality vs throughput tradeoff across INT8(AWQ), GPTQ, and FP8 kernels.

Quick summary of experiments run:
1) single-worker, single-GPU steady-state synthetic replay of mixed-length requests (60% short 8-32 tokens, 40% long 256-2048 tokens), concurrency varied 1-32.
2) same workload but with allocator modes: pooled scratch buffers (default), per-request scratch, and reduced fragmentation mode (large-slab allocator).
3) kernel routing forced: (a) AWQ-int8 tuned kernels, (b) GPTQ kernels, (c) FP8 kernels (low dynamic range fused kernels).
4) quality eval: 200 prompt regression set (mix of instruction-following and long-context QA) with BLEU-like token-match metric + model LLH delta against FP32 baseline.

Testbed details:
- HW: A100-80GB (driver 535.54), NVLink not used (single-socket).
- Runtime: runtime/commit abc1234 (PR 4123), kernel bundle v2.8.
- Model: open-llama-13B variant converted with AWQ and GPTQ pipelines; separate FP8 build from quant-lab toolchain.
- Batching: dynamic batching (time-window 15ms) with continuous-batching enabled.
- Metrics captured: tokens/sec overall, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU SM utilization, L2 bw (GB/s), DRAM bw (GB/s), allocator fragmentation (% free unusable), kernel dispatch wait time (ms), per-kernel avg time/token, quality delta (avg token LLH delta, and exact-match token rate vs FP32).

Representative profiler snippets (aggregated):
- AWQ-int8 (pooled allocator, concurrency 16): tokens/s = 145k, p95 latency = 320ms, SM util = 72%, DRAM bw = 210 GB/s, allocator-fragmentation = 18%, kernel-dispatch-wait = 4.8ms, avg-token-ms = 0.40.
- AWQ-int8 (per-request allocator, concurrency 16): tokens/s = 128k, p95 latency = 420ms, SM util = 54%, DRAM bw = 180 GB/s, fragmentation = 6%, kernel-dispatch-wait = 12.3ms, avg-token-ms = 0.46.
- FP8 (pooled allocator, concurrency 16): tokens/s = 160k, p95 latency = 290ms, SM util = 80%, DRAM bw = 230 GB/s, fragmentation = 20%, kernel-dispatch-wait = 5.1ms, avg-token-ms = 0.37.
- GPTQ (pooled allocator, concurrency 16): tokens/s = 138k, p95 latency = 340ms, SM util = 69%, DRAM bw = 195 GB/s, fragmentation = 12%, kernel-dispatch-wait = 6.0ms, avg-token-ms = 0.43.

Key observations: (raw, unpolished)
- Throughput plateau correlates with allocator fragmentation numbers: when fragmentation > ~15% tokens/sec drops despite SM utilization < 90%. That suggests dispatch stalls due to inability to efficiently reuse large temporary buffers for KV/cache or attention workspace.
- Per-request allocator reduces fragmentation but increases kernel-dispatch-wait and overall tokens/sec drops: we think this is because per-request allocation adds synchronization overhead on critical path (locks) whereas pooled allocator trades fragmentation for fewer locks.
- FP8 had highest tokens/sec but also highest fragmentation: FP8 kernels allocate few large vector temporaries for fused ops which suffer if slab allocator splits.
- AWQ-int8 showed larger p95 spikes for short requests interleaved with long ones: small short requests queue behind large buffer allocations for long requests causing jitter.
- Quality: mean LLH delta vs FP32 (lower is better): AWQ-int8 = -0.28, GPTQ = -0.18, FP8 = -0.05 on long-context prompts. Token-match rate: AWQ-int8 94.6%, GPTQ 96.1%, FP8 97.2% relative to FP32. So AWQ yields biggest quality regression but is not catastrophically worse.

Hypotheses refined:
- Primary bottleneck for throughput plateaus is allocator/scratch buffer packing. When allocator cannot hand out contiguous large blocks for fused kernels, kernel dispatch stalls waiting for buffer coalescing or triggers slow-path remapping.
- Secondary is kernel-level memory-bandwidth: FP8 uses more fused math and reduces compute-bound time, exposing DRAM bandwidth limits in some patterns.
- Quality vs throughput tradeoff: AWQ/int8 remains attractive for cost but needs allocator/work-stealing improvements to avoid latency tail and throughput cliffs in mixed-length workloads.

What I tried to validate these:
- Forced slab sizes to larger values and saw AWQ throughput recover ~9-12% and p95 reduce by ~60ms; fragmentation drops to ~7%.
- Introduced a lock-free per-SM free-list for scratch buffers (experimental) — improved short-request jitter but increased total DRAM bandwidth slightly; tokens/sec improved ~6% on average for mixed workload.
- Synthetic microbench that allocates identical sized temporaries in random order reproduces the plateau reliably (good for regression tests).

Immediate recommendations / playbook items:
- Short term (low risk): increase default slab size for pooled allocator for 13B model families; add a config toggle in serving config so Dedicated customers can tune slab size per model. (owner: Priya)
- Mid term (medium risk): iterate on per-SM lock-free free lists for scratch buffers and try to reduce cross-request synchronization. (owner: eng-serving-runtime infra subteam)
- Long term (architectural): add a kernel-aware allocator layer that exposes requested buffer shapes from kernel invocation so allocator can pack with kernel semantics (coalescing attention KV with fused-FFN buffers). This requires changes in kernel ABI. (owner: serving-runtime + kernels)
- Safety (observable): add allocator-fragmentation metric to Console dashboards (token-level cost correlation) and an alert when fragmentation > 15% for 5m. (owner: observability)

Open questions / TODOs:
- Does NVLink multi-GPU change fragmentation characteristics? We only tested single GPU. (next test)
- How do different inference runtimes' allocators behave (Pytorch CUDA vs our custom allocator)? Need cross-runtime baseline.
- Can we create a cheap runtime fallback: when fragmentation exceeds threshold, force short requests onto a separate worker pool pinned with small-slab allocator? (experiment idea)

Immediate next steps planned:
- Add the synthetic microbench as an automated regression in perf-lab (PR 4123).
- Spike NVLink multi-GPU run and report (Diego)
- Quick UI change: expose fragmentation % in per-model pages (console ticket CON-556).

Notes to self / rough logs:
- 2024-11-16 10:12 Ran pooled vs per-request alloc runs, seed 42. AWQ-int8 showed a weird 12% drop only when long requests > 40% of traffic.
- 2024-11-17 14:02 Implemented temporary larger-slab parameter, saw 9% throughput gain for AWQ with long-context heavy sequences.
- 2024-11-19 09:30 Lock-free free-list prototype ran unstable on low mem machines (OOM spike) — need guard rails.

Appendix: minimal repro steps (for engineers)
1) checkout runtime commit abc1234 + PR 4123.
2) prepare quantized model artifacts (AWQ and FP8) using quant-lab v0.9. See GH:.../quant-lab readme for conversions.
3) run perf harness: perf/harness --model open-llama-13b --quant AWQ --concurrency 16 --mix-file tests/mixes/mixed-short-long.json --alloc-mode pooled --sampling none --duration 10m --profiler aggregated.
4) collect logs: /var/log/runtime/profiler/<run-id>. Use tools/extract_frag_stats.py to get fragmentation % and kernel dispatch histogram.

If anyone wants the raw trace tarballs I pushed them to GCS: gs://redwood-perf/saturation_probe/2024-11-19/ (contact me)
